modules.title: Many-electron  crystal field  and Hund  multiplet
modules.summary: Add Coulomb repulsion, full Hund exchange and pair hopping to a five-orbital fixed-electron-number model, connecting crystal fields, spin and multielectron occupations.

presets.title: d⁶ in a weak crystal field · high spin
d⁶ strong  crystal field  · low spin

lessons.title: From ten single-electron states to fixed-N Fock space
lessons.summary: The many-electron dimension follows fermionic occupations; the number of single-electron levels is not the number of many-electron states.

sections.title: Each spin orbital can be occupied only once
sections.text: Use the five real d orbitals xy,yz,xz,x²−y²,3z²−r², each with up and down spin. At fixed N, select N of the ten spin orbitals to form antisymmetric Slater determinants. Program bitstrings record these occupations, and exchange signs follow from fermionic anticommutation. N=6 gives 210 determinants, not ten single-electron levels multiplied by six.

sections.title: Resolve conserved quantities before computing energy levels
sections.text: This model has no SOC, magnetic field, or spin-dependent  crystal field . Total electron number and Sz are conserved, allowing blocks labeled by N↑ and N↓. The complete Hund spin-flip term preserves total spin SU(2). Diagonalize H within each block, then S² within equal-energy subspaces to avoid arbitrary numerical mixing at accidental degeneracies.

sections.title: At fixed N, what does changing U actually change?
sections.text: This lesson compares the same isolated Kanamori model at fixed N, holding J, the crystal field, coordination, and all other parameters fixed while maintaining U′=U−2J. The coefficient for a same-orbital density pair is U; those for different-orbital pairs with opposite and equal spins are U−2J and U−3J, respectively. Changing U therefore adds the same ΔU to all three types of density terms, rather than changing only the same-orbital repulsion. The occupied spin orbitals contain N(N−1)/2 pairs in total, while the spin-flip and pair-hopping terms proportional to J remain unchanged. The addition in the fixed-N space is thus a constant times the identity: all absolute energies shift together, leaving energy differences, eigenstates, and spin ordering unchanged. This common-shift conclusion does not apply when comparing charge sectors with different N or changing J, the crystal field, ligands, or bandwidth.

sections.title: Read multielectron energy levels and occupations correctly
sections.text: The table groups states with equal energy and S, including 2S+1 magnetic components and possible orbital multiplicity in the degeneracy. Orbital occupations lie between 0 and 2 and sum to N over five orbitals. Trace averages over a joint degenerate subspace do not depend on the eigensolver's basis choice. Complete atomic LS term symbols are not provided here.

lessons.title: Why Hund exchange requires spin flips and pair hopping
lessons.summary: Verify interactions from the analytic two-electron limit rather than relying only on the rule to make spins as parallel as possible.

sections.title: Three density-repulsion terms and two exchange processes
sections.text: Opposite-spin electrons in the same orbital cost U. Opposite-spin density terms in different orbitals cost U−2J; same-spin terms cost U−3J. Additionally, −J S⁺_mS⁻_n exchanges spins between orbitals, while +J P†_mP_n transfers a pair to another orbital. With these terms retained, eigenstates cannot all be identified with fixed occupation diagrams.

sections.title: The zero-crystal-field d² case can be solved by hand
sections.text: For two electrons in five degenerate orbitals, spin triplets have antisymmetric orbital pairs, energy U−3J, and dimension 3×C(5,2)=30. Of the remaining 15 spin singlets, 14 have energy U−J and one fully symmetric doubly occupied combination has U+4J. For J>0 the triplets are lowest; the program checks signs and multiplicities against this full analytic spectrum.

sections.title: Why changing U at fixed N does not change the spin
sections.text: Adding the U coefficients of the three density terms gives exactly the number N(N−1)/2 of occupied spin-orbital pairs. Increasing U therefore shifts the entire fixed-N spectrum and cannot by itself drive a high-/low-spin change in this isolated model. J and crystal-field splitting alter relative energies; charge fluctuations, ligands and bandwidth in real materials require a larger model.

lessons.title: Crystal field versus Hund coupling: from d⁶ spin crossover to the limits of the NiO analogy
lessons.summary: Compare weak- and strong-field many-electron ground states to understand occupation mixing, crossings, and model validity.

sections.title: Two limits of d⁶
sections.text: In an octahedral field, three t₂g orbitals are lower and two e_g orbitals higher. Hund exchange favors larger spin at weak field: the Δ=0.5 eV, J=0.6 eV preset has S=2. At the same N,U,J, the strong-field Δ=6 eV preset has S=0. Pair hopping causes occupations to deviate slightly from a closed t₂g⁶ shell, so use the computed expectation values.

sections.title: Trial occupation diagrams explain trends, not exact critical points
sections.text: The high-spin d⁶ trial determinant has t₂g⁴e_g² and crystal-field energy −0.4Δ; the low-spin t₂g⁶ trial state has energy −2.4Δ. The latter gains 2Δ in crystal-field energy but loses its Hund-exchange advantage. Full pair hopping mixes double-occupancy configurations, so ground states must be compared after diagonalization. Neighboring points on a plotted scan do not determine an exact crossing.
sections.formula: E_CF(t₂g⁶)−E_CF(t₂g⁴e_g²)=−2Δ; the crossover is determined by the full many-electron spectrum

sections.title: NiO supplies physical context, not automatically fitted parameters
sections.text: Local Ni²⁺ in NiO is usually discussed in a d⁸ coordination setting. Multielectron crystal fields require Coulomb exchange, not just a single-electron splitting diagram. Here a simplified Kanamori model with one common J and original teaching parameters is used; the full d-shell Slater interaction has independent angular structure, while ligand hybridization and charge transfer enlarge the space further. The present levels are not presented as a fitted NiO excitation spectrum.
sections.formula: Kanamori(U,J) ≠ complete Slater(F⁰,F²,F⁴) ≠ a ligand charge-transfer model

exercises.title: Count the d⁶ space and determine U's role
exercises.prompt: There are five d orbitals, each with two spin states. Fix six electrons and exclude SOC. Hold J, the crystal field, coordination, and all other terms fixed, varying U′ with U to maintain U′=U−2J. Compare U with U+0.2 eV.

steps.prompt: How many single-electron spin orbitals are there?
steps.hint: Multiply the number of orbitals by the number of spin states per orbital.
steps.explanation: 5×2=10; fermionic occupations are selected among these ten spin orbitals.

steps.prompt: What is the many-electron space dimension at fixed N=6?
steps.hint: The same spin orbital cannot be occupied twice; electron labels are indistinguishable.
steps.explanation: Distinct occupation sets give independent Slater determinants: 210 in total.

steps.prompt: If U increases by 0.2 eV, how much do all d⁶ levels shift together?
steps.hint: This change is not confined to the same-orbital U: U−2J and U−3J also increase by 0.2 eV. Six fixed electrons form 6×5/2 pairs.
steps.explanation: At fixed J with U′=U−2J maintained, the interaction coefficient containing U increases by 0.2 eV for every electron pair. Thus ΔE=0.2×15=3 eV, equivalent in the fixed N=6 space to adding 3I.

feedback.message: At fixed N and J, with U′=U−2J maintained as U varies, count all electron pairs rather than changing a single-particle energy.
The increment 0.2 eV applies to one electron pair; the current occupation contains several pairs.

remediation.prompt: Change to N=3 and ΔU=0.1 eV. Under the same fixed-J convention, what is the common energy shift?
remediation.explanation: Three electrons form 3×2/2=3 pairs, giving a common shift of 0.1×3=0.3 eV.

feedback.message: Multiplying ΔU by the electron count counts particles, whereas the density interaction counts electron pairs.

remediation.prompt: Change to N=4 and ΔU=0.1 eV. What common shift follows when all electron pairs are counted?

steps.prompt: Can changing only U switch the ground state from S=2 to S=0 here?
steps.hint: Fix N, J, and the crystal field, maintaining U′=U−2J. Compare energy differences after applying the same shift to every state.
choices: It depends only on the number of grid points
steps.explanation: In the isolated fixed-N model specified here, every state receives the same shift, so relative energies and eigenstates are unchanged. Changing J, the crystal field, or the charge sector is a different problem.

feedback.message: Raising absolute energies and changing level spacings are different operations. A common shift does not alter the competition between states of different spin.

remediation.prompt: Two energies initially equal 5 and 7. After adding 3 to each, what is their difference?
remediation.explanation: The new energies are 8 and 10, and their difference remains 2. A common constant does not reorder them.

feedback.message: With N, J, and the crystal field fixed and U′ varied together with U as specified here, the common shift preserves eigenstates and spin ordering. Reassess the conclusion if these conditions change.
This is a matrix problem in a finite Fock space. A k-point mesh does not explain the effect of a term proportional to the identity.

remediation.prompt: When adding δI to a finite 2×2 matrix H, is a Brillouin-zone mesh needed to determine whether the eigenvectors change?
choices: No; the original eigenvectors remain eigenvectors
It holds only for a sufficiently dense mesh
remediation.explanation: If Hv=Ev, then (H+δI)v=(E+δ)v. This algebraic relation does not depend on a k mesh.

exercises.title: Derive d² Hund-multiplet energies and dimensions by hand
exercises.prompt: Take five degenerate orbitals, N=2, U=4 eV, and J=0.6 eV, retaining complete spin-flip and pair-hopping terms.

steps.prompt: What is the spin-triplet energy U−3J?
steps.explanation: The triplet energy is 2.2 eV; J>0 lowers it below both types of singlet.

steps.prompt: A triplet has C(5,2) antisymmetric orbital pairs. How many states does this give in total?
steps.hint: Each S=1 multiplet has 2S+1=3 magnetic components.

steps.prompt: Fourteen singlets have energy U−J and the fully symmetric doubly occupied singlet has U+4J. What are these energies?
steps.hint: Multiply the same J by −1 and +4, respectively.
steps.explanation: These singlet energies are 3.4 and 6.4 eV; pair hopping determines the splitting of double-occupancy combinations.

steps.prompt: Which independent count should agree with 30+14+1=45?
steps.hint: Choose two of ten spin orbitals.
steps.explanation: The complete fixed-N=2 space has dimension 45, and level multiplicities must cover the whole space.

exercises.title: Infer trends in spin competition from crystal-field occupations
exercises.prompt: Compare high-spin trial occupation t₂g⁴e_g² and low-spin trial occupation t₂g⁶ for octahedral d⁶; Δ>0, with zero orbital barycenter.

steps.prompt: What is the crystal-field energy of the high-spin trial state?
How much  crystal field  energy does the low-spin trial state gain relative to the high-spin trial state?
steps.explanation: The energy difference is −2Δ, so a larger crystal field favors paired occupancy of lower orbitals.

steps.prompt: For calculated S=2 and S=0, what are the corresponding S² values?
steps.hint: S² has eigenvalue S(S+1), in units of ℏ².
steps.explanation: S=2 gives 6 and S=0 gives 0; the value of S² must not be identified directly with S.

steps.prompt: Can the crossing of two trial occupation diagrams be treated as the exact critical Δ of the full model?
steps.hint: Pair hopping mixes configurations; a finite scan is also not continuous root finding.
choices: Yes; every occupation state is an eigenstate
Yes, provided U is large enough
No; compare the complete spectrum and refine the scan near the crossing
steps.explanation: The full interaction must be diagonalized. This model also omits self-consistent ligand, temperature and structural changes in real materials.

cases.title: Ideal d⁶ ion: from orbital splitting to high- and low-spin states
cases.summary: Keep electron number and interactions fixed, vary only the  crystal field  splitting, and compare ground-state spin, occupations, and the lowest excitation gap.
cases.assumption: No real compound or fitted parameters are specified. SOC, magnetic field, ligand hybridization, and temperature are excluded; a local spin crossover does not determine a real material's transition temperature.

cases.title: NiO context: what does a single-electron diagram omit?
cases.summary: Starting from the NiO coordination and orbital illustration, inspect exchange and many-electron occupations in the fixed d⁸ sector and the S=1 context.
cases.assumption: The site uses a Kanamori model with a common J, not complete Slater multiplets, a ligand charge-transfer model, or an experimental NiO spectrum. Preset energies are illustrative only.

cases.title: Analytic d² audit: verify the model by counting 45 dimensions
cases.summary: Use the complete analytic 30+14+1 spectrum to check Hund exchange, pair hopping, and degeneracy counting, then vary U to identify a common energy shift.
cases.kind: A many-electron benchmark solvable by hand
cases.assumption: Zero crystal field, five degenerate orbitals and a single positive Hund parameter. The listed multiplets belong to the Kanamori approximation; full atomic LS term symbols are not assigned.
